According to the American Bar Association, most personal injury claims settle before trial, and the demand letter is the document that starts that settlement conversation.

A strong demand letter reads as a persuasive legal argument, not a fill-in-the-blank form. It is a tailored legal argument built around the specific facts of your case. Here is what every effective demand letter should contain.

In a Georgia motor-vehicle case, a demand prepared with a lawyer's help is a pre-suit offer under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 (as amended by SB 83, effective July 1, 2024). It must state the amount, give the insurer at least 30 days to accept and at least 40 days to pay, name the parties and claims being released, say whether the release is full or limited, and enclose the medical and other records the insurer needs to evaluate the claim. South Carolina has no equivalent statute.

before: Every demand letter includes a deadline for the insurance company to respond, typically 30 days. The deadline creates urgency and makes clear that if the insurer fails to respond or refuses to negotiate in good faith, the next step is filing a lawsuit.

While there is no blanket pre-suit demand requirement for private negligence claims in Georgia, certain categories of claims do have mandatory notice provisions. If you are bringing a claim against a Georgia city, you must provide written ante litem notice within six months of the incident under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5. A claim against a county must be presented within 12 months under O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1. For claims against the state itself, ante litem notice must be provided under O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26. Failing to send this notice within the required timeframe bars your claim entirely, regardless of how strong the evidence is.

Bad Faith Demand Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6

Georgia has a powerful tool that experienced personal injury attorneys use to put additional pressure on insurance companies. Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, if an insurer refuses to pay a covered claim in bad faith, the insured can recover a penalty of up to 50% of the liability plus reasonable attorney's fees. To trigger bad faith liability, you must send a written demand giving the insurer 60 days to pay. If the insurer fails to pay within that window and cannot show a reasonable basis for its refusal, the penalty applies.

This statute makes the demand letter more than a negotiation tool in Georgia. It becomes a legal mechanism that can significantly increase the insurer's exposure. Insurers take demands structured under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 seriously because the financial consequences of ignoring them are steep.

Georgia's Demand Statute and Its Bad-Faith Penalty

Against the at-fault driver's insurer, Georgia's pressure tool is O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1: an insurer that lets a compliant offer lapse loses the statute's safe harbor for that offer. Georgia also has a bad-faith penalty statute, O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, but it belongs to the policyholder. If your own insurer (on a med-pay or collision claim, for example) refuses to pay within 60 days of your written demand and cannot show a reasonable basis, it owes up to 50 percent of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. It does not apply to a demand on the other driver's liability carrier.

What the at-fault driver's insurer cannot safely do is stall. Failing to acknowledge claim communications promptly, failing to investigate, and refusing a fair settlement once liability is reasonably clear are unfair claims settlement practices under O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34, enforced by the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire.

before:
No Mandatory Pre-Suit Demand for Bad Faith

Unlike Georgia's statutory bad faith framework under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, South Carolina does not have a specific pre-suit demand requirement to trigger bad faith penalties against insurers. Bad faith claims against insurance companies in South Carolina are governed by common law and the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. An insurer that unreasonably refuses to pay a valid claim can face liability for bad faith, but the procedural path is different. There is no 60-day demand window comparable to Georgia's statute.

That said, sending a clear, well-documented demand letter still matters in South Carolina. It creates a paper trail that demonstrates the insurer had full knowledge of the claim and chose not to settle, which strengthens any subsequent bad faith argument at trial.
after:
South Carolina's Bad-Faith Rules

South Carolina has no demand statute for claims against the other driver's insurer. Its bad-faith remedies belong to the insured. Under S.C. Code § 38-59-40, an insurer that refuses to pay its own insured's claim for 90 days after demand, without reasonable cause or in bad faith, owes reasonable attorney's fees. The courts also recognize a tort claim for bad-faith refusal of first-party benefits (Nichols v. State Farm, 1983) and for a liability insurer's failure to settle within policy limits (Tyger River Pine Co. v. Maryland Casualty Co., 1933). Toward a claimant, the insurer's duties (acknowledge communications promptly, investigate, settle in good faith once liability is clear) come from S.C. Code § 38-59-20 and are enforced by the South Carolina Department of Insurance.

That said, sending a clear, well-documented demand letter still matters in South Carolina. It creates a paper trail that demonstrates the insurer had full knowledge of the claim and chose not to settle, which matters twice: it documents the insurer's failure to act for a Department of Insurance complaint, and a within-limits demand the insurer refuses is what exposes it to its own insured if a verdict later exceeds the policy.
